# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Movies that completely shift genres halfway through

**Score:** 66
**Body:** I love movies that start as one thing (like a grounded drama, romance, or comedy) and then pull the rug out from under you, completely changing their genre mid-way through. From Dusk Till Dawn, Parasite, and Audition are classic examples. What are some other movies that pull this off masterfully without spoiling the shift in the marketing?

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Full Metal Jacket

Edit: apparently I have been punked by an AI bot - but let that not spoil our discussion
2. Barbarian.  I honestly thought there was something wrong the streaming service.
  - When the guy finds the basement and he's asking Google if it can count as livable square footage is one of the funniest scenes I've ever seen in a movie, comedy or not.
3. * Unbreakable 
* You're Next
* Dark City
* One Cut of the Dead
* Sunshine
* The Prestige
* Cabin in the Woods
* The Descent
4. Sunshine (2007)
5. Sorry to Bother You
6. The Prestige.

Probably not exactly what you mean, but “oh hey, let’s do science fiction” is a shift, though it works with the theme.
7. Bone Tomahawk
8. The Perfection 

From Dusk Til Dawn 
  - From Dusk Till Dawn is the classic blueprint for this, that's why I included it in the post! But The Perfection is a wild pick. Which of the two did you enjoy more?       

## 2. Project hail Mary is such a good movie man

**Score:** 59
**Body:** so yesterday I watched project hail ma and man the cinematics and the story and everything, literally everything was so perfect man , ryan gosling made a masterpiece , what are y'alls favourite space movies?

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The book is awesome too!
  - Not only is it awesome, but it's amazing if you like hard science and a ton of geeking out on science. The movie cut out a significant amount of science. Rocky also does a lot more than just watching the main character do stuff compared to the movie.
  - Good to hear that. I’ve got the audiobook, but not listened yet. 
2. A sci-fi movie being this warm without losing the science is what got me.
3. Rocketman with Harland Williams
4. If you're partial to this sort of thing. There's a Project Hail Mary sequel fanfiction that is very good. It's about Grace returning to Earth.

[The Long Journey Home](https://archiveofourown.org/works/68584716)
5. Space Cowboys was pretty good.
6. I enjoyed the book version of Project Hail Mary but thought the movie was too easy of a crowd-pleaser to really find interesting or say anything remarkable. However, to be fair, the book itself is also a crowd-pleaser and quickly glosses over any sort of grit or edge, so the tone of the movie is true to the tone of its subject matter, and my hangups are entirely personal. 

  
That said, my personal favorite space movie, taking my personal hangups into account, is Dark Star from 1974. The film achieves a unique, "spaced out" nihilistic workplace-comedy sort of tone that's darkly humorous and I find very resonant. That film keeps creeping up my personal best-of list, it's in the top 10 for sure. 


7. It's definitely my favourite space movie. I think space sci-fi movies often focus too much on the technicalities and spectacle that they forget about the human core at the center. Interstellar had this in parts. JK Abrams' Star Trek trilogy also had it in parts. 

But PHM is the only space movie I've seen where the human core was at the forefront of the story. I never thought a space movie can be this warm and heartfelt. 
  - It had so much heart 

## 3. Movies that are so dark and edgy that they end up being silly and ridiculous (Intentionally)

**Score:** 51
**Body:** So I was looking into "grimdark" and something I vaguely remember reading was that the concept of "grimdark" wasn't supposed to be serious and that the joke is that everything is just really dark and edgy and serious for no reason whatsoever.

And I was wondering what films are like this where they push up the dark edge levels so high that you can't take it seriously anymore. I mention intentionally in my title because I want the ridiculous edginess to be an intentional choice rather than something that came as a result of poor writing.

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Very Bad Things. 1998. It is truly ridiculous.
2. Sin City
3. American Psycho
4. The Lobster maybe? If I’m understanding the question correctly!
5. Man Bites Dog exemplifies this with its ridiculous dark humour and self awareness but you really don't get films going over the boundaries like this anymore. I believe the 1st time film makers never made another movie after this however it also pioneered the found footage format well before the Dogma 95 manifesto. Surprisingly I think it's uncut on YT.
6. Your mileage may vary and maybe I’m not fully understanding the assignment here but the Terrifier movies are like that for me. The gore is cranked up so impossibly high that it’s impossible to take seriously, and they get funnier with each sequel. 
  - The second Terrifier really revels in the extreme violence but I found the third got a bit slapstick but still fun. 
7. Heathers

Teeth
8. Natural Born Killers. I feel like it was made for teenagers sneaking into R-rated movies. It's so silly yet takes itself so seriously that I have a hard time seeing it appeal to adults. 
  - I fear that you may have failed to understand the film. It’s very much meant to be a dark comedy, and that sense of humor doesn’t at all take away from its themes of media glamorization of real-life murderers.

# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. The Truman Show gets more disturbing the older you get

**Score:** 976
**Body:** When i first thin about The Truman Show, I think of it as a clever and entertaining movie about a man discovering that his entire life is a television show. 

But the older you get, the darker the idea become. 

Truman isn't just being watched- his entire environment, career, and choices have been carefully controlled since birth, all for someone else's entertainment. The fact that everyone around him know the truth makes some of the movie's quieter moments feel especially unsettling.

And yet, the movie never becomes completely cynical. Truman's decision to leave is ultimately about choosing an uncertain reality over comfortable lie. 

Do you thing The Truman Show has become more relevant with time, or was it always meant to this unsettling?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. the quiet moments with his wife doing product placement hits way harder now that we all live inside algorithm shaped bubbles
  - Prob my fav scene in the movie 
    - What are you talkin’ about? Who are you talkin’ to!
      - Somebody do something !!! Then his neighbor knocks on the door with a six pack lol
2. His life wasn't comfortable, it was profoundly dissatisfying in a way he eventually could no longer ignore
  - Exactly. The comfort was really just an illusion, and once he realized that, he couldn't unsee it
3. It was always meant to be unsettling, and yes, all the implications are messed up. Not just for Truman but for everyone involved.

Like, that actress playing Truman's wife, does she get any time off? Does she have time for other acting roles? A personal life? How would they justify her absence to Truman without him getting suspicious? It's not like the cameras stop rolling either, his life is basically a 24-7 show.

And what about the kids who grew up alongside Truman and went to school with him? Was he the only member of his class to stay in his hometown? Clearly not, given his best friend is still there, but surely others have stuck around too, 'cause if too many left, then that means Truman might want to join them and leave too. That means at least some of those kids spent their entire childhood, adolescence, and a good chunk of their adulthood living this fake existence, collectively lying to their one schoolmate who didn't know what was going on. How fucking messed up is that?? Did any of those kids feel bad about their complicitness in keeping a human being in perpetual prison?
  - If it was in real life I can imagine a scenario where when he leaves the show, he then files a class action lawsuit and then settles with the networks for an undisclosed amount, maybe around 120 million dollars with him and other victims as plaintiffs. Perhaps another scenario is that it proceeds to trial and a lawsuit eventually bankrupts the network, like what happened with Gawker 

I would assume after that, also Congress passes some law banning Big Brother type-shows without consent of the participants. And Truman testifies in Congress against the dangers of these type of realities. He marries actress-crush and gets divorced amicably 10 years later for "differences". And, after that, he becomes a YouTuber.

Initially Cristof's career doesn't take a hit. He manages to produce programs in Bravo TV, mentoring Andy Cohen who surpasses his teacher. After a Netflix documentary in 2015 with the whole saga, he's the forced to resign, and now lives a quiet life no longer in the entertainment industry, hoping people will forget.
4. Always meant to be super unsettling.  
5. I remember seeing this when it was in theaters and came out thinking "Cristoph is one of the worst villains I've ever seen on screen". That opinion has only solidified over time.

## 2. What are your thoughts on Ryan Gosling as an actor?

**Score:** 311
**Body:** I see a lot of people call Ryan Gosling overrated and say he can’t really act, or that he basically plays the same character in every movie and relies on the same facial expressions. I honestly disagree. I really like him as an actor, and I think a huge part of his appeal is just how much charisma he naturally has on screen. He doesn’t always have to do a ton or completely transform himself to make a character interesting, sometimes his presence alone is enough to carry a scene.

He also reminds me a lot of those classic Hollywood stars from back in the day, where being a great movie star wasn’t necessarily about disappearing into every role, but about having that undeniable screen presence and personality that makes you want to watch them. Gosling has that quality imo. Whether he’s playing someone quiet and emotionally withdrawn in *Drive*, a more vulnerable character in *Blue Valentine*, a goofy comedy role in *The Nice Guys*, or something completely different like Ken in *Barbie*, he brings something that makes the performance memorable.

I wouldn’t say he’s one of the greatest actors of his generation or anything, but I think he’s a genuinely great actor and an even better movie star. Even when he’s playing characters that are somewhat similar, I rarely find him boring to watch. There’s just something about his screen presence that works for me.

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Generational comedic talent. Waste that we don't have three more Nice Guys films already. 
  - didn’t think about how classic hollywood star presence works here
2. When I first saw him I thought “oh another handsome guy actor” but he’s surprisingly good actor with range , especially love his comedy and light-hearted ones. Currently “Project Hail Mary” is my favorite film of his 
3. Guys got range 
4. Very good actor. Would almost use a word that I dislike (underrated) for his acting chops. He used to be a pretty face typecast guy, but he has real range. 
  - He’s so low key and non-showy, you almost forget about him between films. But I’ve never seen in a role that I didn’t like.
5. Drive 
6. The fact that we never got a nice guys 2 is the crime of the century 
7. Great actor, great range, and importantly, he takes interesting, diverse roles. Also, he can laugh at himself, and modesty isn’t always in high supply among Hollywood’s elite.
8. Favourite actor

Watch Lars and the Real Girl and Half Nelson

## 3. Masters of the Universe 2026

**Score:** 222
**Body:** Ok I'll take the heat on this.

Saw this last night after being sceptical following reviews so didn't see it in the cinema.

This is actually very well done, it has all the glorious 80s cheese but with quality fit for the 2020s.

The humour in it is also actually great, to the point you have to double check what was actually said such as "fist these guys, and give them head" in the context of fighting but the characters themselves are well aware of what they just said.

The only thing I don't get about this is.. it has Idris Elba and 4 other British actors.. playing, essentially aliens from another dimension and they have to put on the American accents.

But this was a genuinely enjoyable movie.

Jared Leto as Skeletor, I didn't actually know it was him but was well played.

This movie is not serious at all but it's great. I loved it.

1. I don't think there's heat to take. Everyone who's seen it really liked it. Just no one actually went to see it.

Though we should really wait for Jarnathan before making the comparison official

2. I saw it at the cinema and loved it. I'm 46 so I guess I'm the target demographic, if you're not familiar with the original cartoon there are bits that just won't make sense.
  - I'm 40 and had the toys.. just one of those things that's been lost to time.

I was expecting something like transformers tbh, just CGI battles and Linkin Park tracks.

But nope.. fantastic Queen tracks and Techno Glam Rock and endless cheese. Even Skeletor was cheesy and funny. It's great.
3. I nearly shed a tear of joy, when he tranformed for the first time.
  - I'm an old man who was lucky enough to get a Castle Grayskull as a kid when they came out. We didn't have much money and I got few other toys, but I did not care. I watched that cartoon religiously.

I had to pause the movie and take a breath during that scene to fight back a tear.

I liked the other movie, but this one made me feel like a kid watching it.
4. So much fun.  Trapjaw was sick
5. I absolutely loved it, I thought it was hilarious. Had me laughing out loud all the way through. It is a shame that it didn't fare better at the box office.
6. This movie delivered what I expected, escapism with 80s style. I am no Leto fan but he crushed Skeletor, this is on my to own list.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Directors who have a strong grasp of quality control?

**Score:** 67
**Body:** List filmmakers you believe possess a solid grasp of quality control? Most are hit-and-miss, but some are practically incapable of making a bad film. Even a mediocre one is extremely uncommon coming from them.

I think Martin Scorsese is a prime example of someone who gets it. You could argue that he rarely, if ever takes any wild swings, but when his films are so consistently good with the occasional masterpiece (or near) it doesn't matter.

What are your thoughts? 

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Tarkovsky only produced masterpieces. I don't think Bresson has produced a bad film also. I think Hawks is incredibly consistent, considering his career span for more than four decades and thirty features.
2. My gut feel on this would be Kubrick. Without an encyclopedic knowledge of his process, my understanding is that he was incredibly exacting about every aspect of the process, and watched the "finished" film over and over, making changes surprisingly late. 

The memes about his punishing way of dealing with actors and reshooting scenes endlessly would corroborate this. I'd love if somebody better versed in this could weigh in and support or dispute this feeling. 

Anecdotally his oeuvre feels like something that has been very well quality controlled. 
  - There’s an old story about Scatman Crothers that highlights Kubrick’s obsession with perfection. Scatman had to perform his death scene in The Shining 40 times, leaving the 70-year-old actor emotionally drained and physically exhausted. Kubrick would have opted for even more takes had Jack Nicholson not stepped in and convinced him to stop. 

There’s another scene in The Shining where Scatman explains the shine to Danny Torrance. That scene set the Guinness World Record for the most takes (148) for a single scene with dialogue.

Immediately following The Shining, Scatman was tapped to star in Clint Eastwood’s Bronco Billy. On his first day of shooting, when Scatman realized that “one-take” Clint was not going to put him through the same grueling process that Kubrick had, he broke down on set and cried tears of relief.
    - To be honest I'm really not convinced that that obsessive number of retakes is what makes SK's films great.  To me it just seems wildly inefficient and a sign that, for all his filmmaking expertise, he was not great at directing actors - he was good at casting great actors but not necessarily at directing them because there is a big difference.  Plenty of other filmmaking greats such as Kurosawa, David Lean, and Fellini were able to to capture cinema brilliance without wasting everyone's time.
      - I think it has a bit more to do with “method directing” i.e. using psychological manipulation to push actors to the absolute brink in service of the shot. Perhaps that’s what Kubrick was striving for, capturing those moments and expressions on film where an actor ceases acting and is just exhibiting raw human emotion. Friedkin employed the same sadistic approach in The Exorcist, slapping Father O’Malley directly before a take and hiding guns around set that he could fire off at random to elicit genuine terrified reactions from the actors.
  - I never forget reading Job Ronson's article where he was invited to Kubrick's house after his death and found piles of boxes. Boxes contain stuff from his movies. And I mea- in one box there where Polaroid pictures of front doors all across London. Apparently Kubrick was looking for a good door for a shot in Eyes Wide Shut. The shot was couple seconds long and there ware approximately 30k photos in the box.

Also there was a library room and all the books where about Napoleon. Kubrick wanted to make movie about Napoleon. No wonder he only made a few movies with this approach.
3. > You could argue that he rarely, if ever takes any wild swings

Are you serious? What do you consider Kundun, or The Last Temptation of Christ, or The Wolf of Wall Street? Even Hugo or Killers of the Flower Moon were huge swings in their own way.
4. David Lynch, *Dune* really did a number on him and he had final cut privileges on every film he made after. As a fan of him it's hard to be objective but that said I appreciate his overall approach even with the films he did that I didn't love as much. 
5. I'd say Jonathan Glazer's films are quite high quality. Also Tom Ford - curious to see "Cry to Heaven" when it gets released. Both these guys haven't released many films, seems like quality over quantity
6. I see “quality control” as part of but not the same thing as making a good movie. Whether a movie is good or bad is too subjective. This thread proves that—people in here can’t agree on which Scorsese movies are good or bad.

When I think strong grasp of quality control I think of directors like Fincher and Kubrick who are known for obsessing over details like minutia related to set dressing that may never be on camera. Like Fincher having the prop department fill out John Doe’s obsessive notebooks in Se7en or Kubrick making sure the books and CDs stacked around the apartment in Eyes Wide Shut make sense for the couple. Or how Fincher will employ CGI to correct nearly imperceptible wrinkles like digitally altering strands of hair or how an actor’s hair is parted in Gone Girl and Girl with the Dragon Tattoo. And everyone knows about their endless takes in an effort to find the perfect line read or to perfectly recreate the way they hear it in their heads.

I also think of writer/directors like the Coens who meticulously write dialog to include every umm and ah and grunt etc. They’ll call cut and redo a scene if an actor says “I, uh, well” instead of “Well, I, uh” as written. William H. Macy talks about how difficult it was filming scenes in Fargo where Jerry is stuttering and stammering and stopping himself mid sentence. It was all written like sheet music with zero improvisation allowed.

## 2. Manhunter (1986) Final Cut re-release: stuff added and removed

**Score:** 47
**Body:** I couldn't find a decent post/thread about changes to Mann's new 4K Final Cut of Manhunter. I saw it last night, so thought I'd post observations about the changes for anyone else who's curious. Have put some own thoughts in italics. I'd be keen to hear anything I've missed, or corrections about versions, from anyone who's seen it. I've had a bunch of versions over the years, and struggle to remember which versions have which scenes.     

\- title card is now white, rather than green.   

\- credits play over the opening beach scene, rather than black fading to blue/beach scene.     

\- added intro to FBI discussion scene (where guy shows contructed teeth), Will/Crawford sitting, then Will being introduced with his thoughts about the killer's motives being based around illusions/dreams *(nicely sets up FBIs general resistance to Will, which pays off when Will is right about the prints on the eyes).*   

*-* a short snippet added to Lecktor's cell scene, can notice the slight change in visual which is a bit distracting.   

\- removed scene just after plane scene, where Will is inside Jacob's house with the realtor (Miami Vice guy). Plane now cuts straight to Will outside the house (with the cool Shriekback-Evaporation music). *(seems a good choice, the realtor scene doesn't add anything and the weird dolly up to the door before opening always felt more like a Sam Raimi shot).*   

\- removed scene just before the night set-up scene with the jogger, where Will is with Molly in bed. Molly remembering when they first met and saying "time is luck". *(I like the vibes of this scene, but think it works better without).*   

\- added back the scene where Will compares Dollarhyde as a child, says "as an adult, someone needs to block the sick fuck out of his socks". *(Am glad this found its way back, I never understood why it was removed after earlier VHS versions).*    

\- removed the nice shot just after climax, where Will/Crawford are at a dock at sunset.    

\- left the dir cut ending with Will visiting the family that would have been next. *(Seems included to suggest that Will's needing to "see" the family reinforces his parallels with Dollarhyde, but it just seems mad that the FBI would even tell the family they were going to be next, with the father now all nervous and gun-wielding. I'm not a fan of this scene).*  

*-* end beach scene now truncated. Molly asking "did they make it?" and Will "most of them" is now dubbed over them standing by the sea, rather than by the turtle pen.   

Some slight changes to colour-grading, and probably loads more little edits that I didn't notice.   

I'm used to seeing Manhunter in 4:3 open matte ratio, and while it was nice to see it at the cinema, its mad how much the 2.35:1 ratio cuts off. Like the flaming wheelchair scene is perfectly shot in 4:3, but in 2.35:1 it just looks like a couple of seconds of fire filling the screen.   

Would be keen to learn of any more changes that anyone noticed? 

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Was the scene in the grocery store with his son new or changed? I noticed that the aisle they're in changes without any progression. In one shot the shelves around them have boxes of cereal or candy or crackers or something, but then suddenly, between switching shots from Will to his son, the shelves around them are all coffee, which allows his son to ask the question about what kind of coffee Will likes. It's a bit jarring and weird if you're paying attention to the background of the shelves behind them.
  - I don't think that scene has changed. They walk forward twice while talking. The first time when Will's talking about being in hospital, the aisle behind Kevin changes to flat packs (sugar or something), the second time when he's saying about having to think like Lecktor to catch him it shifts to coffee.  
  - I noticed that on TV recently. I assumed a continuity error.
2. People have been talking about the differences, but the main thing I noticed was just how amazing Manhunter looks. Manhunter always looked and felt like a TV Movie and the VHS copies that were available  post Silence of the Lambs were incredibly grainy. The THX DVD release was a serious improvement, but the 4k restoration blows everything out of the water. The movie popped for me  in a way it hadn’t before to the point it felt like I was watching it for the first time. 
  - Manhunter has always looked good. But VHS and bad DVD transfers have always looked bad. Even the prior Blu Ray releases for this film showcase such a beautiful evocative picture.
  - Huh, I've had the UK VHS ex rental and a late 90s VHS and never felt it looked grainy or TV movie-ish at all. Glad you liked the 4K though.  
3. Ahh, I love this movie so much! Nice write up. I think I might be one of the few of the controversial opinion that Brian Cox's Lektor is better than Hopkins's version. I mean I understand Hopkins is the definitive one, but I just love the visceral hate and molten stewing aimed at Will that Cox does just under the surface of his performance.
  - I agree! With Cox's version you actually believe he could eat someone. Hopkins/Mikkelson were great but they're too self conscious and eager to impress. Cox had that banality of evil thing, he wasn't trying to impress, and scarier/unnerving because of that. 
    - Yeah, I think all the actors brought their own special sauce to the material, but Cox just feels like a caged tiger and it's so enthralling!
  - His is the only Lector that I don’t find cartoonish or otherwise goofy.

## 3. Thoughts on Blue Is the Warmest Colour

**Score:** 34
**Body:** **My take**

When I first watched it, I felt sad for Adèle. This time I still feel heartbroken for her, but I could also relate to Emma more. Or rather, I could relate to both of them better, and I understood Emma in a way I hadn't before. Maybe I was drawing on real-life experiences.

They were so young when they met, and they were together for years. The timeline isn't clear, but this is how I read it:

\-They meet: Adèle is 15 or 16, Emma is 20 or 21.  
\-They see each other casually, then become a couple: Adèle turns 18, Emma 22.  
\-They move in together, and Adèle is already a teacher: about four years later, so Adèle is 22 and Emma is 26.  
\-They break up and meet again at the café: I feel they should be older here, so Adèle is 25 and Emma is 29.  
\-The gallery opening happens maybe a year or less later: Adèle is 26.

That makes a span of about 10 years.

## 4. Primetime and the pathology of showmanship

**Score:** 14
**Body:** I watched Primetime over the weekend and I’ve been thinking a lot about what it was trying to say and do with its (many) bold artistic choices, from the grimy hyperstylized visuals, to the heightened and weirdly comedic tone, and of course Pattinson’s delightfully crazy performance. The natural temptation, given its subject matter, is to judge it as a direct examination of Chris Hansen, To Catch a Predator, and the social/legal/ethical ramifications of his work. Most critics have taken this approach, either enjoying the film as an entertaining recreation of Hansen’s show or deeming it thematically inferior to the “Predators” documentary from last year, which was a more sober assessment of the show’s consequences. Some reviews I read have even questioned what the point of this movie was if it didn’t adequately reckon with its subject, suggesting that its lurid, gonzo style makes it merely the same kind of trashy, exploitative entertainment that TCAP itself was.

But I think a lot of this misses the movie’s actual interest: showmanship, and America’s pathological drive to treat anything as fodder for it, indeed including child sexual abuse. The story of Chris Hansen just happens to be the perfect vessel to explore this theme. And the key to all this, I think, is that Chris Hansen isn’t actually the movie’s protagonist. Decoy Dan is.

Not only is Dan the only character who really gets an “arc” (compared to Pattinson’s Hansen, who is an unhinged egomaniac from the first minute and stays there for the whole movie), but the final scene focuses on him rather than Hansen. Specifically, him getting his SAG card (the validation for all the effort and ordeals he went through) and being asked the final question of the film: “Are you an actor?”

Skyler Gisondo’s face in response to that question is the movie’s whole thesis in one frame. Yes, Dan realizes, he is now officially an actor. What was his breakout role? Literally being used as bait for actual pedophiles.

Primetime is hence a movie about filmmaking itself: about the transformation of reality into performance. The satire lies in the fact that the material its characters use for their “creative process” is the real sexual predation of children. Think about it: this guy Chris Hansen took the most depraved and heinous crime in the world (an “ancient evil” in his words) and somehow managed to repackage it into an entertainment product for people to “tune in” to, while rebranding himself from a milquetoast journalist into a self-styled superhero and meme, complete with his own “catchphrases”. All the actual “pedo-catching”, of course, was done by Perverted Justice and the police; Hansen just turned it into this trashy public spectacle, in the form of what was essentially an extremely morbid prank show. He became arguably the first circus showman for pedophilia.

So many of the movie’s other choices make sense through this lens. It literally opens on Hansen “practicing his lines” like an actor on set (indeed, in front of an actual Hollywood-style makeup mirror), except the lines are real texts sent by pedophiles to who they thought were minors, and his “scene partner” is the pedophile himself. (Notice the little smirk on Hansen’s face when Tony Revolori’s predator gets on his knees and begs not to be put on TV, like he’s pleased at how well his “co-star” is nailing the “role” assigned to him.)

There’s also the scene of Decoy Dan arriving at the sting house, which initially looks like a film set (crew everywhere, makeup, cameras, lights) only for them to vanish and the whipped-cream pedo to enter, instantly turning the house from a stage to the scene of an actual crime in progress. The shock and horror on Decoy Dan’s face when the guy whips out his dick is completely valid on its face, but also represents the jarring shift from fiction to all-too-ugly reality, a line famously blurred by TCAP. 

Of course, once Chris meets Dan and sells him on what he’s doing, we see Dan start coming around to Chris’ way of thinking, as he too begins harvesting his sordid reality for art. He watches episodes of Inside the Actor’s Studio, and bugs the TCAP producers to send him dailies of his “scenes” to review later, all like a serious actor practicing his craft. I'd argue that Hansen’s actual function as a character in the movie is to represent the endpoint of the transformation we see Dan experience over the course of the film.

Dan's arc culminates in that surreal, possibly-imagined scene of Dan literally trying to impersonate Hansen when confronting the guy with crutches. As an aside, that whole scene seems to act as the movie’s most direct indictment of TCAP itself. Everything from the target having a disability, to the fact that Dan flubs his lines and then stares blankly afterwards, seems to represent his a-ha moment regarding a point people often make against the show nowadays: that it’s all one very manufactured, expertly rehearsed performance, while all they’re doing is mostly ensnaring developmentally-disabled men who represent the lowest hanging fruit of child predators. It's definitely not 100% true, but at least partially.

Hansen himself is snapped firmly back to the reality side of the equation in the film’s climax, when their “whale”, the DA, shoots himself in the head. Nothing quite as real as that. The last we see of Hansen, he continues murmuring his lines back to himself in a pseudo-catatonic state. His final line, the famous “What would have happened if I wasn’t here?”, evidently doubles as a statement on Hansen’s own role in the media landscape. Given that it’s the last thing he asks himself before going quiet, perhaps he too means it that more meta way: it would make it the one pang of self-reflection we get from him for the whole movie.

(His paranoia about the affair doesn’t count as self-reflection. He’s more worried about the scandal making the CHARACTER of Chris Hansen look like a hypocrite than owning up to his actual wrongdoing as a man. He has nothing to say to his actual wife after all, even once she finds out. And the one time we see his kids, he forces them into the role of the audience to his performance, waking them up to watch the latest TCAP episode. Again, it’s all about the role, never reality. Life is but a stage for the character he can't seem to turn off, and the perpetual wackiness of Pattinson's performance, even in small or private moments like that hilarious mouthwash scene, reaffirms this.)

As for the movie's supernatural-horror flourishes, with Hansen’s visions of a demon from his nightmarish trip to India, one review I read suggested it contradicts the film's portrayal of Hansen as solely motivated by ratings, but I’d say even this element of the film is consistent with its showmanship thesis. It mirrors the way actors wax poetic about their work as this noble endeavor, a higher calling, even if all they’re doing is playing pretend. After all, Hansen's speech to Decoy Dan about “cleansing the world of an ancient evil” sounds a lot like the grandiose shit actors say when accepting awards; he even gives Dan a shiny totem to hold while telling his story and asking him to imagine himself experiencing it. Hansen’s trauma is surely real, but it also serves as a convenient way for him to frame his craven exploits and self-styled superheroics as a moral good with a greater purpose.

The last, more meta layer of all this comes back to the movie’s whole cinematic style. Visually, it amps up the gaudy VHS aesthetic of the mid-2000s. Pattinson’s own performance is turned up to 100 in every scene, and virtually every line out of his mouth is a meme in the making (or, hell, has already been made.) And of course, it's directed by a documentary filmmaker who has spent his career blurring the line between reality and narrative, with style as his primary tool. I have less to say about this except to suggest that this too is very likely an element of satire: framing Hansen and his life through the same trashy lens as the show (and era) he helped create. If we see this movie as being about entertainment itself, then its own cinematic language is as much a piece of that theme as its actual contents.
